app_summary: An online shop selling astronomy products, based on the OpenTelemetry Demo. It is built with polyglot microservices (Go, Java, .NET, Python, Node.js, Rust, ...) communicating via gRPC and HTTP behind an Envoy frontend-proxy, with Kafka for asynchronous order processing and Valkey as cart store. Supported Operations: View product catalog, Receive product recommendations and ads, Add item to cart, Checkout with selected items, Currency conversion, Process payment, Generate shipping quotes, Send order confirmation emails

final_report.root_cause: There are two distinct, co-occurring problems observed in the incident: (A) Application-level failure in the shipping integration: the checkout service sent a request that the shipping service rejected with HTTP 400 (validation/contract mismatch). This caused the checkout flow to fail and surface 500s to users. The shipping service was reachable and its pod healthy, but it returned 400 for the failing requests (http.request.body.size=150) and its logs do not emit validation error details, preventing more precise attribution of why the payload was rejected. (B) Intermittent network/connectivity failures (ECONNREFUSED) between the Envoy/frontend-proxy (and other callers) and upstream services (frontend, recommendation, cart). Multiple traces show gRPC UNAVAILABLE / connection refused to cluster IPs (examples: ECONNREFUSED 10.96.130.78:8080, 10.96.87.220:8080). Investigation shows Envoy (frontend-proxy) appears to have initialized clusters and the upstream service pods and Service resources are healthy and listening; therefore the connection-refused events are network/transport-level (e.g., kube-proxy/CNI/iptables, kube-proxy stale state, or intermittent Envoy endpoint resolution/state) rather than application-level port-binding or pod crash. The shipping 400 is the proximate cause of the checkout failures; the ECONNREFUSEDs are a separate but concurrent availability problem that affected other flows.

Shipping pod logs contain only INFO messages (no validation error details). 5) The combination of healthy pods/services plus ECONNREFUSED in traces indicates the connection refusals are intermittent network/transport layer problems (not pod not-listening), while the shipping 400 is an application-level request/contract mismatch.
final_report.investigation_summary: Priority-driven investigation results: - Priority #1 (frontend-proxy logs & pod): frontend-proxy pod is Running; Envoy clusters initialized; pod logs do not show repeated outbound ECONNREFUSED or explicit upstream target attempts — disproved hypothesis that proxy logs contained direct evidence of misrouting. - Priority #2 (service name/port alignment): frontend proxy expected 'frontend' and Service 'frontend' exposes 8080 with an endpoint — no name/port mismatch. - Priority #3 (frontend pods): frontend pod is Running/Ready with tcp readiness on 8080 and no restarts — not the cause. - Priority #4/#5 (recommendation): recommendation pod is Running and logs show it is listening/handling requests; Service has endpoints — not the origin of port-bind failure. - Priority #6/#7 (shipping): trace evidence conclusively shows shipping returned HTTP 400 on POST /get-quote (http.request.body.size=150) which propagated as a checkout error; shipping Service/pod is reachable and healthy, so root cause here is application-level (payload/route/Content-Type or contract mismatch). Cross-cutting observation: traces show connection refused to various cluster IPs that do not match the ClusterIPs observed via kubectl_describe in the investigation, indicating intermittent or inconsistent network-level failures; the investigation did not find a pod/service misconfiguration that would explain these ECONNREFUSEDs, so the network layer (kube-proxy/CNI/iptables or transient Envoy endpoint state) is the likely locus for those failures.
